canonical_topic: Negative Prices Break Risk Management Systems
definition: Negative prices tend to break risk management systems built assuming prices are positive; diagnosing the resulting problems can be time-consuming and confusing, since a portfolio can show a large percentage gain while losing real dollars, and the calculating software is still functioning as designed.
core_idea: Risk systems often carry implicit positive-price assumptions, and negative prices (which do occur in power markets) can produce confusing or misleading outputs even when the system itself has no bug.
key_points: Negative prices can cause a portfolio to appear up in percentage terms while actually losing dollars — described as confusing but not a software defect.
The author flags this as a common source of long, confusing debugging efforts in trading risk systems.
trading_implications: Risk and P&L systems handling energy (especially power, which can go negative) should be explicitly tested against negative-price scenarios rather than assuming positivity.
caveats: Assuming a percentage-based P&L read (e.g., 'portfolio up 10%') is a reliable signal — under negative prices it can diverge sharply from actual dollar gain/loss.
